title: Baptism, two ways
hookLine: many churches baptize infants into the family; Baptists and others baptize believers who choose

lines: A BABY OVER A STONE FONT.
A MAN WADES INTO THE RIVER.
cards: Two scenes, one Sunday. In the first, a baby in a long white gown is held over a stone font. She has no idea what's happening, and may be yelling about it.
A priest pours water over her head three times and says her name aloud, and the whole congregation promises to help raise her.
In the second, a twenty-five-year-old in a T-shirt wades into a pool at the front of a church, or into a river. He tells, in a few sentences, why he's there.
The pastor lowers him all the way under and brings him back up, dripping, to cheering. Both churches call it the same thing.

teach.b: Baptism, from the Greek baptizō: to dip, to plunge, to immerse.

teach.h: IN THE NAME OF FATHER, SON AND SPIRIT.
teach.b: Nearly every Christian tradition baptizes, pointing to Jesus's own command at the end of Matthew's gospel, in the King James Bible: "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost."

Almost all churches baptize with water, in that threefold name, and for most it happens once. The big difference is when. Catholics, Orthodox Christians, Anglicans, Lutherans, Methodists and Presbyterians baptize infants.

Grace comes first, they say, before we can earn it or even understand it. A baby is brought into God's family the way she's born into her own. They point to Acts, where whole households were baptized together.
Orthodox Christians immerse the baby three times, then give chrismation and communion right away.
Baptists, Pentecostals and many other churches baptize believers, people old enough to choose. In the New Testament, they say, people heard, believed and then were baptized.

teach.h: WHAT DOTH HINDER ME TO BE BAPTIZED?
teach.b: They point to an Ethiopian official in Acts who sees water by the road and asks: "See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?"
For them, baptism is a public yes, and full immersion pictures dying and rising with Christ. Each side has its texts and reasons, and some families include both.
In many traditions, baptism is also when your name is spoken over you; that's why some still call a first name a Christian name.

how: Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran, Methodist and Presbyterian churches baptize infants with water in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit; Baptist, Pentecostal and many other churches baptize believers who ask for it, usually by full immersion.

o: a vow adults take before getting married in church
a feast held when a new church building opens
being dipped in or washed with water in God's name

games.q: you're an official from Ethiopia, riding home, and you've just heard the good news explained. your chariot passes water by the road. what do you do?
o: make a note to be baptized when you get home.
ask: see, here is water; what hinders me?
keep riding and think it over.
games.why: he stops the chariot, goes down into the water and is baptized there. believer's baptism churches often point to this story.

practice: Say your own first name, quietly, and notice that someone gave it to you: spoken over water in a church, written on a form in a hospital, or a name you've since chosen for yourself.
If you were baptized, you might remember that day or who was there. If you pray, give thanks for whoever named you; if you don't, just hold your name as a gift.

wordCard.voice: Baptism. From the Greek for dipping or immersing. Water and a name, for infants in many churches and for believers in others.
